claims.text: The initial alloy is an induction-melted, non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy contains heterogeneous metastable Mg-rich solid-solution regions interspersed with coarse intermetallic compounds.
SPS accelerates decomposition of metastable Mg-rich solid solutions.
SPS produces a more uniform dispersion of fine intermetallic compounds.
SPS refines the alloy's grain structure.
Rapid SPS treatment promotes rapid atomic diffusion and non-equilibrium phase transformation.
SPS reduces the size and heterogeneity of Mg-rich regions.
Refined and redistributed intermetallic phases preferentially nucleate and grow a coherent oxide layer during high-temperature exposure.
The modified phase distribution promotes in situ formation of protective oxide scales during high-temperature oxidation.
Redistribution of intermetallic phases alters localized electrochemical sites and corrosion-attack pathways.
Relative to conventional processing, the SPS-treated alloy will form a more uniform and protective high-temperature oxide scale.
Relative to conventional processing, the SPS-treated alloy will have altered, potentially improved or more predictable, corrosion behavior.
The untreated or conventionally sintered baseline has larger and more heterogeneous metastable and intermetallic phases.
The heterogeneous baseline microstructure causes less uniform oxidation and variable corrosion performance.
The proposed mechanism applies to Mg-containing alloys with density below 6 g/cm3 when SPS does not produce complete equilibrium.
Extended thermal exposure may override the microstructural stability conferred by SPS.
Long-term corrosion behavior may depend on small variations in alloy composition and processing parameters.
